raw_text: {"translation": "The use of drugs for human beings often arises simply for this alone, namely their heating or cooling or moistening or drying, or their acting according to some combination of these; but sometimes it arises for their tightening and drawing together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relaxing what has been tensed, or rarefying what has been condensed, or condensing what is porous, or softening what is hard, or hardening immoderate softnesses, or emptying what is full, or filling what is empty, or effecting some other such thing. response.translation: The use of drugs for human beings often arises simply for this alone, namely their heating or cooling or moistening or drying, or their acting according to some combination of these; but sometimes it arises for their tightening and drawing together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relaxing what has been tensed, or rarefying what has been condensed, or condensing what is porous, or softening what is hard, or hardening immoderate softnesses, or emptying what is full, or filling what is empty, or effecting some other such thing. For a person who has been chilled, not only the physician but any layman whatever, led by the very nature of the matter, desires to find a heating drug, and likewise one parched by a fever of the ardent (causus) kind desires a cooling one. So too any layman whatever who has a sodden ulcer bids the physician dry it, and if it is dry and without moisture, moisten it. And indeed, when they perceive dryness together with heat throughout the whole body, as those who have been scorched by the sun and those who have been fatigued long to bathe and drink cold water, they contrive to find whatever is capable of moistening and cooling at once; and many of the laymen, led by nature itself, do often provide themselves with the remedies for these conditions.

response.translation: Yet for inflammation and scirrhus and oedema, for erysipelas and putrefaction, for herpes and gangrene, none [708] of them any longer attempts to seek the cure for himself, since each such condition is by now too great a matter for a layman's judgement and requires some more august knowledge; and they call such knowledge medicine, and the one who practises it a physician. They themselves advance only so far as to know that the hollow ulcer needs filling with flesh, the foul ulcer cleansing, and the level ulcer cicatrization; but they do not know the drug that fills with flesh, or cleanses, or cicatrizes. In the same way, if they have a muscle or a tendon that is hard or tense or slack, they know precisely that the hard one has need of softening drugs, the tense one of relaxing drugs, and the slack one of tightening drugs; but they do not know the drug that softens or relaxes or tightens. Finding such things is the work of the physician alone. For as far as heating and cooling, moistening and drying drugs go, one can find some of the laymen sharing with the physicians in the discovery of drugs; but in the matters just mentioned, all of them are entirely without experience.

response.translation: Concerning the power of such things I have treated in the four commentaries preceding this one: in the first and second, refuting the arguments of the sophists and showing the true method, by using which one might discover the powers of drugs; in the third, having left the sophists aside, I went through from the beginning all the logical questions, by going through which most thoroughly and, as one might say, by being made skilled in the art (technōtheis), one will be competent to discover the powers of all drugs; and in the fourth I made my discourse concerning the sensibles proper to the [710] tongue, which they call flavours (chymoi), showing how someone setting out from there might discover the primary qualities and powers. I also touched, so far as need called for it, on the olfactory qualities at the end of the book, showing how much it is possible to obtain from that source too towards the discovery of the primary powers. But in this present fifth book I propose to expound another class of powers, secondary, as one might say, and tertiary, in addition to the primary ones that are common to all things. For since each of the particular things is not mixed from those in the same way, one of them, I think, has become relaxing, another tightening or softening or hardening or rarefying or condensing.

Further, on the basis of the effects (ἔργα) which they are naturally disposed to produce, they have been said to have in them powers that are rarefying and condensing, softening and hardening, clogging and cleansing, drawing and repelling, and besides these relaxing, tightening, opening the mouths of vessels, contracting, thickening, thinning, anodyne, pain-causing, concocting, bringing to suppuration, dispersing, [711] sweat-inducing, stupefying, numbing, sleep-inducing, causing derangement, putrefying, burning, corroding, eschar-forming, liquefying, compacting, producing bad humours, tempering, purgative, checking, roughening, smoothing, obstructing and unblocking. And when they proceed still further and name them, as it were, individually after each of the effects, they call them diuretic, emetic, evacuant downward, laxative, errhine, phlegm-expelling, bringing on the menses or checking them. Likewise also either generative or extinguishing or provocative or retentive of milk and of semen. And still more, when they name certain powers hepatic or splenic or aural or ophthalmic or dental or sciatic or nephritic or podagric or arthritic or pleuritic or for cough or stone-breaking, they arrive at the particular powers. In the same way it has also been said that there is a flesh-forming power for an ulcer, and a scarring one, and an agglutinating and a removing one. Indeed, it is scarcely even possible to enumerate all the particular powers if we attempt to name them after each of the things they bring about.

response.translation: Hence none of the parts undergoing scirrhous hardening is cured either by the drugs that dry vehemently, or by those that heat strongly, [727] or by those capable of both. For the drugs that heat vehemently, having violently dispersed the moisture lying alongside and contained in the parts, dry out what remains, so that it becomes incurable. The drugs that dry vehemently, even if they do not heat, and not through the intermediate step of evacuating the fine-particled part, nevertheless bring the flux wedged in the scirrhous parts to the extreme of dryness, directly and in accordance with their own nature. Only those drugs, then, which heat, but not vehemently, and at the same time do not dry strongly either, cure such conditions. Such drugs are called softening, since they do both things at one and the same time: they liquefy what has been congealed and disperse it little by little. raw_text: {"translation": "For this reason mandrake and hemlock, henbane and poppy too (I mean now the herbs themselves), if one uses them moderately, are condensing [752] in their powers; if more liberally, not only condensing but by now numbing as well; and if most liberally, no longer only numbing but by now also deadening. The substance of the things contrary to the anastomotic [drugs], being coarse-particled and cold, is that of all the astringents that are without admixed pungency. Sufficient examples of their material have been given in the fourth book, in which I also explained the substance of such drugs as being earthy and cold. It is therefore no longer anything to wonder at if this substance alone is naturally able to draw together and close the mouths of the vessels that have opened contrary to nature. For to it alone is present everything that the things to be drawn together require. response.translation: The other is that of the so-called cold drugs, when, employing unmixed cooling, they numb [765] the part; and numbness is very nearly an absence of sensation. Those drugs that stop pains by healing the condition could not reasonably be called anodyne, for this belongs in common to all things that treat. Truly anodyne drugs, then, must be fine-particled and not much hotter than the moderate ones, so as to evacuate, disperse, rarefy, thin, concoct and even out whatever has been caught and shut up within the parts in pain: pungent, viscous or thick juices; many juices obstructed in narrow pores; or also some vaporous and thick, or considerably cold, pneuma that has no suitable outlet.

There must therefore be absolutely no astringent power at all in them, not even if the place or the affection should additionally require it. From this it is clear that sometimes they will in no way benefit the condition but will only soothe the pain, in which case they will also be called truly anodyne; but sometimes they will also give some additional benefit to the condition itself and will have a twofold power, being at the same time an anodyne [766] and a healing drug. These matters too will be discussed more fully in the books of the Therapeutic Method. For the present it is enough to explain that, of these drugs specifically named anodyne, some, as has been said, belong to the first rank of the heating drugs, and these are indeed truly anodyne, such as dill oil; others are [hot] to a degree close to that of our own body itself, such as those called suppurative, whose materials have been discussed earlier. Their use will be determined in the books of the Therapeutic Method. Those, however, that produce torpor when drunk, and for this reason are called anodyne and soporific by most people, are of a mixture most opposite to the truly anodyne drugs. For they all cool the body and numb sensation to such an extent that, if a little more is drunk, it brings on death. The best of them for the use in question are those that dry.

The former, then, are of the same kind as the purging drugs, the latter as those that generate milk and semen, about which we shall speak a little later, after we have first gone through the cough drugs, since these too are named in two ways: some from producing coughs, others merely from stopping them. Their powers are most opposite. For some are of a thinning nature, the others of a thickening one. The thinning power, then, arises in hot and fine-particled substances, the thickening power in cold and coarse-particled ones. Let this discussion end here. It is proper to pass on to the one postponed a little earlier.

raw_text: {"translation": "And indeed the drugs that correct such a condition of the stomach have been called 'digestive' (πεπτικά). In the form of their designation they are not [780] analogous to the 'sharp-sighting' ones, but in their effect and in their power they are closely similar. Since we said that some powers have also been named from parts of the body, it would not be amiss to go through these as well. For they are neither suited, as one might suppose, to all the affections of the part, nor to a single one in such a way as to benefit nothing else. Rather, they got their designation from the part either because [they are used for it] most often, or because they act most of all upon that particular part. response.translation: And indeed the drugs that correct such a condition of the stomach have been called 'digestive' (πεπτικά). In the form of their designation they are not [780] analogous to the 'sharp-sighting' ones, but in their effect and in their power they are closely similar. Since we said that some powers have also been named from parts of the body, it would not be amiss to go through these as well. For they are neither suited, as one might suppose, to all the affections of the part, nor to a single one in such a way as to benefit nothing else. Rather, they got their designation from the part either because [they are used for it] most often, or because they act most of all upon that particular part. They are called ophthalmic because we use them both most of all and most often on the eyes. Such are the collyrium made from roses, the one made from pompholyx, the one called Cnicus, the Libanium, and all the others. It is possible to use these also when the ears are affected, and the mouth, the nose, the genitals and the seat, though neither so often nor so beneficially. Again, [we call powers] hepatic, splenic, pleuritic and stomachic because we see these, too, benefiting each of those mentioned most of all and most often.

What the cause of the benefit is [781] will be stated in the treatise on the Therapeutic Method, in which we also go through everything else concerning the use of drugs, so that there is no need to lengthen the discussion here any further, except perhaps to remark briefly on the use of names which certain others of the more recent physicians introduced as innovators, and not least the so-called Methodists. For that they speak of certain 'checking' (stalticai) powers, that is, constricting, or drawing together, or repelling, or something else of that kind, is neither absurd nor obscure. But when they say that certain materials or powers are 'metasyncritic', what is said is neither clear nor true nor proper to their sect, since they claim to avoid the indication taken from dogmatic suppositions, for, they say, the apparent novelties suffice them. But that, when the pores of the body are turned aside from the natural state into the unnatural, certain affections arise according to the particular character of their alteration, is a dogmatic supposition.

These things happen with good reason. For since the cold draws together the substance of whatever it touches, and condenses and constricts it, it is necessary, first, that in this process the thin fluids are excreted, [622] as tears from the eyes and coryza from the nostrils; and then it also appears biting to these parts, though in a different manner from the hot. For it is not by eating through what is continuous, but by tearing it apart, that the cold is at once painful and biting; hence it does not appear such to hard bodies either. For when soft things are drawn together and compressed, it happens both that their fluid is squeezed out and that their parts are torn apart: the fluid, as in a sponge drawn together and compressed by our hands; the tearing apart, as in things that are divided and torn apart, whether by us pulling with our hands or by something else. For something of this sort must also be suffered by rare and soft bodies under the action of the cold, since their rarity readily admits the chilling within, and the soft parts in the depth are still more readily congealed by it.

Entering, then, through each of the pores in rare bodies (such as are all ulcerated parts, and the eyes, the nostrils, the mouth and the parts about the stomach), the cold lays hold of all the parts of the bodies being cooled and, as it were with many [623] grips all round, gathering them together and compressing them, tears them away from the parts continuous with them. In this affection, then, not a few empty spaces must come to be, not only because the thin fluids are pressed and excreted, but also because the soft substance is drawn together into a smaller place. But an empty space cannot arise in continuous bodies while their continuity is preserved. If, then, one does arise, it is clear that this continuity is destroyed and the continuous body is torn apart; and in this the affection of sensation that is at once distressing and biting presents itself. Yet the quality of both is not the same, of the things that bite by cooling and of those that bite by heating. In the former we at once also have a perception of the substance being drawn together and constricted; in the latter, a perception of its being dissolved and diffused. Moreover, the speed is not alike in the two affections: with cooling things the biting is somehow slower, whereas with heating things it passes through most swiftly.

Now whatever is sour only is in every case cold, whether a pear, or an apple, or sumach, or the fruit from brambles, or that from the mulberry, or that from the pomegranate, or any other whatever, be it fruit, or juice, or plant, such as oxylapathon and oxalis, which they also call oxys. For if, when you taste it, the sourness in it shows itself strong and distinct, while nothing of pungency appears in it, you will find this flavour cooling in every case, and you may use it with confidence, whether you wish to use it for causus, applying it over the hypochondria, or for erysipelas, or for any other hot affection. In the same way you will also clearly find all the cold diseases harmed by it. But when the quality appears to you mixed, then with pungency one must also suspect heat, and with astringency some other kind of coldness. For sour coldness is fine-particled, astringent coldness coarse-particled.

response.translation: Since, moreover, [638] at the beginning, while still woody, as Theophrastus also said, they are at once dry and acerbic, and it is the quantity of the moisture flowing in upon them that makes them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is more earthy and the sour one moister. And we in addition to these points shall rightly say that such a flavour is also cold in its mixture. For if it were only earthy, it would be clogging, not acerbic; and in a way the argument, having now passed over to the very substance of the flavours, lays hold of scientific demonstration.

For if the acerbic juice clearly has the property of contracting, drying and roughening the tongue, and it was shown in the preceding discussions that bodies are contracted, constricted and compacted by cold alone, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is altogether cold. And since it also dries unevenly [639] (for this was what roughens), it would also be altogether earthy. For the watery passes evenly through everything, since it belongs to it inseparably to unite again, even if it is torn apart; whereas the earthy body carried along in the juices is already subject to being torn apart, and it is also its property no longer to come together easily. Moreover, the sensation proper to each of the two affections, once you recall it, will bear witness to the same conclusions. For the passage of sour flavours through the sentient bodies is seen to take place quickly, and that of acerbic flavours slowly. And sour things are seen to act more in depth, acerbic things on the surface. All these things, then, indicate that acerbic bodies are coarse-particled and that sour ones are fine-particled.

raw_text: {"translation": "Chalcitis, then, and misy [641] and chalcanthus and copper scale and sory, being at once astringent and biting, act according to both qualities upon each of the bodies they come into contact with, but they cannot teach us clearly whether they have their burning through the astringency or through the pungency. raw_text: {"translation": "it too certainly partakes of sweetness, provided at least that such things are not precisely acerbic, as oak-gall and sumach are; nevertheless, for these very reasons their use is already rather [651] that of drugs than of food. At any rate, women suffering from the craving of pregnancy (kitta), those who are replete, and those whose stomach is slack are seen to desire to taste such things, whereas those who are hungry, on the contrary, turn away from both acerbic and sour things, but take to sweet and oily things and long to be filled with these. Now the oily itself is, of course, also sweet, and everything that nourishes belongs to the genus of sweet things. And this holds of them with good reason, and in accordance with the very substance, so to speak, of food. For nutrition is the replenishment of what has been evacuated. raw_text: {"translation": "Those so affected need to be soothed without violence, as has been said, and not to acquire from outside any [660] biting heat or pungency. These matters, then, already in some way touch upon the therapeutic method, which in many places shares common ground with the present treatise; and for this reason let us leave them and return again to the matter at hand. Now the juice of the unripe grape is not only sour but also acerbic. For, as was also said before, nearly all the fruits of trees in their first growth, as Theophrastus too used to say, are acerbic to those who taste them; then, when they are filled with moisture, they take on sourness and lose some of their acerbity. But neither what is added nor what is taken away is equal in all fruits, neither in respect of their species nor in respect of their genus in any way. response.translation: For it has already been stated and demonstrated many times, [668] but it will nonetheless be stated once again, what it is to act or to be acted upon in respect of whole substances. And it seems I must recall it now as well, so far as suffices for the present matters, starting from somewhere about here. The generations of all individual bodies come from the four elements, and they are unequal and differ in their mixtures. For some have more fire than of the other elements, some more water, others, as it may happen, more earth, and some more air. From such inequality, then, the particular characters of the individual bodies were brought about: those of plants from the elements themselves, and those of animals from the plants, as has been shown in the discussions on the elements. Some things change into one another directly, others through other intermediate things. For example, earth changes into wheat and barley and the other things of that kind, and each of these in turn into human flesh; but it is not possible for the earth itself to become flesh by passing over the change that lies in between.

It was necessary, therefore, I think, that some organ should be produced by nature for animals that discriminates the similarity and dissimilarity of substances, so that, recognising their natures, it would choose what is proper and flee what is alien. This, then, is the tongue: by the exceptional degree of its sensation it has discernment not only of cold or hot or dry or moist things, but also of things proper and not proper. For into this part alone six nerves are implanted, whereas each of the other parts has received a share of either one or two, and not even these so large. And since some things are more proper to the nature of our body and others less, and some are in this pairing of the mixture and others in that, of necessity the gustatory qualities came to be more numerous.

And this happens with good reason. For what is extremely sweet, and for this reason no longer admits any addition of sweetness, must change into the next quality in order; but to what is deficient, completion accrues from concoction. response.translation: [684] For those people need things that are astringent and viscid, not things that cut and divide. These matters, however, already in some way touch upon the therapeutic method. Having now defined the power of the bitter flavours, and having said that they are cutting, thinning and cleansing, and clearly hot to such a degree that they do not yet burn, let us in our account go on once more to the pungent ones. And first let us say that they are strictly hot, then that they are corrosive, caustic, eschar-forming and colliquative: all such are so when applied to the skin. When taken inside the body, however, those that are most opposite in their whole substances to certain animals are all putrefying and deleterious to those animals. Those that are so only through the immoderation of their heat are ulcerating to the inner parts if they are coarse-particled and earthy. If they are fine-particled, they are diuretic and sudorific, and, to put it simply, cutting and dispersing.

For this is the most fine-particled of all those mentioned, just as is also the flower of the Asian stone. For this too is sufficiently fine-particled, but less hot than aphronitre. Hence it also melts away overgrown flesh more painlessly, whereas the flower of nitre already bites it, and aphronitre bites it too, and no less does nitre itself, even though it is less hot than those. But it has also been said earlier that coarse-particled substance corrodes more, provided, that is, that it partakes of some heat. For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as happens with fine-particled substance; instead, being held back, always remaining and lingering, and staying for a longer time at one place in our body, it reasonably becomes distressing, like a stake fixed in the flesh. Since what is fitting has been said about all the flavours, it would remain still to speak also about vapours.

response.translation: For not only are they not pleasant to those who taste them, but they also display no small amount [698] of bitterness. And yet the bitter was never fragrant, nor pleasant to us either as a drug or as a food. What, then, is the cause of this disagreement? Theophrastus too inquired into it, but it is perhaps better that we also say what we know about it. The generation of the bitter flavour was shown to come about from sweet things thinned by heat, and bitter things are evidently hotter and more fine-particled in their mixture than sweet things. Moreover, the sensation of smell takes place in the very ventricles of the brain, as I have demonstrated about these matters elsewhere, and the substance of the objects of smell is vaporous. For the things that flow off from bodies, mixing with the surrounding air and then being carried into the brain by inhalation through the nostrils, move the sense. Reasonably, then, all things that are odorous are also hot, for an abundance of vapours depends on heat. Yet it does not follow at once that everything odorous is also pleasant, because not everything is akin to the pneuma in the ventricles of the brain.

raw_text: {"translation": "But since it is not possible to aim at all those who read [these books], since they are unlike not only in their natures but also in their ages and conditions, in the two books before this one I adopted that form [542] of discourse which seemed likely to be most useful to the majority: in the first I examined the power of vinegar and water, and in the second I went through mostly matters concerning oil, adding a few things about rose oil as well. In this third book I shall give the discourse the form I had resolved from the very beginning to undertake. response.translation: For it is surely possible both to crown oneself with roses, and at some time, having pounded them, to apply them as a poultice to the mouth of the stomach of a person suffering from burning fever, and, [559] having squeezed out their juice, to sip it down, and, having mixed it with water or oil, to rub some one of the parts of the body with it. But out of excessive cleverness Herodotus the physician does not even admit that rose oil with vinegar, which they call specifically oxyrhodinon, cools us. Then, remembering at least this much, that he himself uses it at the beginnings of phrenitic diseases, and perceiving the contradiction (for it is agreed by nearly all physicians, down even to the followers of the most insensate Thessalus, that at the beginning one must repel and cool rather than heat and relax), he says that it does not cool but is astringent. And yet there would have been no difficulty, when he too had at some time been overheated (for he was a man subject to the same affections as we are), in moistening his head with oxyrhodinon and learning by experience the action of the drug.

raw_text: {"translation": "[560] And it would have been very easy, I think, for him also to use it at some time when he had been chilled, pouring it over the head, dropping it into the ears, pouring it into the nostrils and rubbing it over the whole forehead, just as we use marjoram oil and iris oil and the other warming unguents. For indeed, by his account, oxyrhodinum heats in no merely moderate degree, being compounded of two very hot drugs. raw_text: {"translation": "When, therefore, a small substance having a vehement power, mixed with another substance that is abundant and has a weak power, arrives inside the body, it escapes the notice of the taste, but it accomplishes its work [578] more effectively than that other substance. These things too are marvelled at by the many, and they consider it a matter without explanation if some astringent body is naturally such as to purge, for example aloe, flake of copper and burnt copper; for, they say, these ought on the contrary rather to check the belly, not to urge it on. But that the apple, as it may happen, which is astringent, purges when taken with scammony, at this nobody marvels; and yet, starting from this, it would have been very easy, I think, to infer in the case of aloe too that there is some mixed power. And if it were possible to separate in it what purges from what does not purge, as we do in the case of milk and cabbage and a great many others, it would no longer be marvelled at. response.translation: In the case of juices, at any rate, it was said earlier too [582] that the heaviest part in them is one thing, the lightest another, and a third something else again, mixed through the whole juice. And it is nothing surprising if in the juice of the rose as well there is a heaviest part, analogous to amurca and lees, and a lightest part, this too analogous to the flowers that ride on the surface of each of the juices; and a third, such as the fermenting part in must; and besides these a fourth, the most unmixed and purest part itself, of which these three are the residues. Thus, then, we also store the juice of the rose, by mixing it with honey, or by boiling it together with oil, or by steeping the whole roses in them.

But that in this too it is plausible that the four kinds are present, both the [583] proper [part] of the juice itself and the three residues, is plain to see, and above all because the matter of their quality is not simple. Rather, the rose will seem to you to have some astringency as well, if you should wish to chew it thoroughly; and it also has a certain sweetness and, as it were, a slight biting. Yet even if none of these were apparent to those tasting it, it would have been enough to conceive of the admixtures of the other juices from the fact that it is not completely astringent. For if the harsh [juice] were alone, it would be extreme; so that, if it is not extreme, neither is it alone. For whatever origin of astringency you may suppose, if you conceive of it alone, without the others, coming to be present, this must necessarily be rendered extreme; just as, if heat alone were to come to be present in some body, such a thing will be completely fire. For the admixtures of contraries break down the extremes.

raw_text: {"translation": "Something of this sort [587] happens also when a harsh and a nitrous power come together into a single flavour, whether nature itself has mixed them or some physician has compounded them. For the tongue perceives the quality of each of the two flavours at one and the same time; and if it perceives them, it is clearly also disposed according to their proper powers. Each of the other parts of the body must likewise be affected in the same way, even if it does not perceive the qualities. For one must not suppose that the tongue differs from the other parts in being affected or not being affected, but in that none of its own affections escapes it, owing to the precision of its perceptive faculty. Its looseness of texture also contributes to this. raw_text: {"translation": "If, however, you take some lump of one of them, whose outer [607] surface has been chilled by the external and surrounding air, you will reasonably perceive no heat at all. For you are touching those parts of it that have been chilled, and doing so before breaking it up into fine pieces. In the same way, in winter, well water, or spring water of some other kind, has often appeared warm to those touching it; but if someone touches it after first warming his hands, it will appear cold. response.translation: If, however, you take some lump of one of them, whose outer [607] surface has been chilled by the external and surrounding air, you will reasonably perceive no heat at all. Let this, then, be said as a kind of digression by the way. But those things which, on coming into contact with us, kill either by erosion or by putrefaction (for it was about these that the discussion was) are reasonably supposed to be deleterious to the human constitution in their kind, and not, like cooling things, in quantity only.

For these are sometimes even overcome and become nourishment for the animal, whereas things that putrefy, even if they are taken in the very smallest bulk, are in every case corrupted, since all things capable of putrefaction putrefy [608] when they are heated and moistened, and the blood is hot and moist. Putrefactive drugs, therefore, can never cease from putrefying and from causing putrefaction in turn. And for this reason some of them kill a very long time after they have been taken, and especially those that are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances. For these settle in our bodies, and then, putrefying in the course of time, they eat through the neighbouring parts of the animal and corrupt them along with themselves. For the more fine-particled ones may even be excreted at times together with the residues; and it is for roughly these two causes that some of the drugs that kill by putrefaction and erosion have on occasion not killed. One is the cause I have just finished stating: when they happen to have been excreted together with the residues before harming the body. The other is when the person who took them is somehow fortunate enough to make use of foods, or of things that would in other ways have benefited him, or of some physician supervising him, if it so happened.

I am not unaware that it is not possible to follow such arguments adequately for those who have not been trained beforehand in the commentaries on the natural faculties.

response.translation: These matters too are demonstrated [616] at greater length in the [treatise on the] Causes of What Is Evacuated. One must suppose that some such affection befalls the veins in excessive purgations. While at the beginning both the opening of the orifices and the weakness are still moderate, what is thinnest and less proper is excreted; but when both have advanced further, then the thick things too, and those most proper to the animal, are evacuated. For this reason, then, yellow bile is excreted first, phlegm second, black bile third, and last of all these in excessive purgations the blood: this as the humour most proper to the nature, while before it the thinnest is first and the thickest last. Now the order of their evacuation has also been stated by Hippocrates in the book On the Nature of Man, but it will be stated now as well, so that nothing may be lacking to the account. For if you give a drug that is an evacuant of phlegm, in excessive purgations the yellow [bile] is evacuated first, the black second, and the blood last. But if the drug should be an evacuant of yellow bile, the phlegm will follow, the black [bile] third, and the blood fourth.

Moreover [617], if it should be purgative of black bile, it will evacuate that first, after it the yellow, then in this way the phlegm, and last of all the blood will follow, flowing out as if from vessels already lifeless, since great weakness has seized them and their mouths have reached the utmost distension. From this it is clear that in excessive purgations the humour most proper to human beings is evacuated last, and each of the others according to the degree of thinness or thickness it happens to have. The cause of the humours that are not proper to the purging drug being excreted at all lies in these three things: the weakness of the vessels, the width of their mouths, and the biting of the purgative. For when the vessels are no longer able to hold the humours within themselves, and their mouths are opened wide, and the drug continues to irritate but no longer has its proper humour to draw, it is altogether necessary that the others be excreted in the order stated.

raw_text: {"translation": "For perhaps the biting alone, if it persisted, would have sufficed to rouse the organs to excretion, but much more so when [618] opening of the mouths and weakness of the vessels concur together. response.translation: For although they do not know why white hellebore purges upwards and black hellebore downwards, [477] nor why cnicus is an evacuant of phlegm and epithymum of black [humours], they nevertheless use the drugs for those purposes which experience has taught, and they treat those in need, and they trust what is plainly apparent, and they laugh at those who construct the contrary by reasoning. But Archidamus, besides despising in many matters what is plainly apparent, seems to me to deserve blame in this respect as well. For he says that dry rubbing is better than rubbing with oil, because [oil] renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas in those who are rubbed dry it becomes softer. Yet, going on a little further in this very argument, he no less says that pieces of wood and hides and the other things rubbed with oil let it pass through to their very depth, and that this is the greatest testimony that in our bodies too it passes inwards, blocks up the pores, and prevents the outflows of the fluids. And I, for my part, do not know how these statements agree.

response.translation: For no one warms the oil beforehand or [480] chills it beforehand in snow; each takes whatever comes to hand and rubs down straps and hides with it. In the same way, I think, the masters of the palaestra (paidotribai) rub down the boys with whatever oil comes to hand, neither warming it beforehand over a fire nor chilling it beforehand on snow. Indeed, we ourselves have not infrequently cooled a burning head by pouring very cold oil over it. And if the oil has no salt in it either, it will cool still more; and if it is also pressed from unripe olives (ōmotribes), very much more still. raw_text: {"translation": "For most physicians do not, it seems, [485] go about correctly either testing drugs or reasoning about their power. response.translation: For most physicians do not, it seems, [485] go about correctly either testing drugs or reasoning about their power. One must test only those that are unmixed and free of every acquired quality: first on the best constitution of the body, next also on ill-tempered bodies, and then likewise on simple diseases, as has been set out both in the preceding book and in the third book On Mixtures. And one must reason while always distinguishing what is incidental from what is primary and per se. Some physicians go wrong not only in these matters but also in their opinions about the affections. Take oil, for instance: almost everyone agrees that it is a remedy for fatigues, but they no longer agree about what sort of affection fatigue is. One says that it is a dryness of the joints, which have been drained of their moisture in the movements; another adds the dryness of the muscles as well; and yet another, contrary to these, says it is a great moistness together with tension and warmth, because a flux has come upon the parts that were violently moved.

raw_text: {"translation": "Another blames not a quantity of fluids but [486] a quality alone, saying that in the more immoderate movements certain colliquations take place of fat together with soft flesh, of which one part is dispersed outwards by transpiration, while another part is retained in the body, and this, being pungent and biting, produces the, as it were, oil-like condition. So that, even if it is agreed that lassitudes are treated by oil, the fact that the condition of the body is disputed allows nothing firm to be inferred about the power of oil. And this has happened not only in the case of lassitude, but also whenever we give oil to drink on account of pain, or biting, or inflammation, or inject it through the anus, or pour it over the part. response.translation: So, when the philosophers say that oil is hot [510] and put forward as no small proof of this, as they think, the speed of its change into flame, some, contradicting them, say that this does indeed belong to it, but because it is fine and airy; whereas from its congealing quickly in winter it clearly indicates its coldness. For it is overcome by the cold more readily not only than wine and vinegar but even than water itself. Others, contradicting these, concede that it is airy, and say that this is plainly apparent from its lightness, but they do not agree that it is also cold in its power. For all air, they say, is hot in its nature, as its generation also shows: water, when thinned and dissolved by heat, becomes air. And it is clear that from this point a very great question succeeds to them, one disputed even among the most renowned philosophers, Aristotle and those under him supposing air to be hot, and those from the Stoa supposing it to be cold.

raw_text: {"translation": "For it could not help, because it does not heat strongly, and it was not capable of harming, because it did not cool at all; but once it has taken on a strong acquired heat, it [appeared] to help sufficiently: whenever we set those so affected into tubs [523] of hot oil that have certain roots, or heating herbs, boiled in them. Hence, with good reason, it is as it were a kind of material for the other drugs. For if you mix cold things with it, the mixture will be cold, and if hot things, hot. For whatever is of the middle mixture serves each of the two extremes, so that, if it should be mixed with something hot, it is not able to render cold what is mixed from both, since it is not itself cold either; nor, if [mixed] with something cold, [to render it] hot, for neither is it hot. And on this account, with good reason, some declare that it heats us, others that it does not heat. response.translation: For it could not help, because it does not heat strongly, and it was not capable of harming, because it did not cool at all; but once it has taken on a strong acquired heat, it [appeared] to help sufficiently: whenever we set those so affected into tubs [523] of hot oil that have certain roots, or heating herbs, boiled in them. For whatever is of the middle mixture serves each of the two extremes, so that, if it should be mixed with something hot, it is not able to render cold what is mixed from both, since it is not itself cold either; nor, if [mixed] with something cold, [to render it] hot, for neither is it hot. And on this account, with good reason, some declare that it heats us, others that it does not heat. For it would seem to heat in that it arrives at a warmth equal to that of the body that heats it; at any rate in this respect it is able to heat in return. But in that it does not further increase the heat which it found, it would not seem to heat. response.translation: There are three sources of a dispute of this kind: failing to distinguish the classes of the things said to heat [524] us, using homonymies confusedly, and leaving no mean. Now, the things said to heat us are both those hot in actuality, like fire itself, and those hot in potentiality; and of the things hot in potentiality some heat as foods, some as drugs, and some as coverings. And 'hot' itself is the name we are accustomed to give both to what is already such in actuality and to what is such in potentiality, as has often been said before as well. But the hot in actuality includes what is hot simply, such as fire; what is hot by predominance, such as the animal; what is called hot when compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus; and what is called hot when compared with any chance thing whatever. The hot in potentiality is, first, distinguished in opposition to the hot by accident, and then, next, it has as many differences of meaning as the hot in actuality has. For since it is, as it were, a material suited to what is hot in actuality, one thing would be the proper material for the things called hot simply, another for those hot by predominance, and yet another for those called hot when compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, or with any chance thing whatever.

response.translation: [379] Galen, On the Mixture and Power of Simple Drugs, Book 1. How great a benefit it is to know precisely the powers of simple drugs, both for the compounding of complex drugs and for the timely use of those already discovered, I do not need to show now. For the former will be demonstrated in the books On the Composition of Drugs, the latter in the writings of the Therapeutic Method.

But what follows next after the treatise On Mixtures, that is what will be stated here, [380] once we have first distinguished the meanings of the expressions and of the names that we shall use in this discourse. We call a drug, then, everything whatever that is capable of altering our nature, just as, I think, we call food whatever is capable of increasing our substance; for both belong to the category of relation. The simple drug has itself been so named by way of its contrast with the compound, and it is that which holds unmixedly to its own nature. A power is a certain active cause. Of this, one kind exists in actuality, the other in prospect. In actuality there is the power of heating in fire and that of cooling in ice. In prospect there is the power of heating in pellitory and castoreum and the like, and that of cooling in henbane and mandrake and similar things. That there is some power, then, hardly anyone will dispute: in purgative drugs a purgative power, in emetic drugs an emetic power, in sternutatory drugs a sternutatory power, and in cough drugs a cough power, and so for each of the other effects a power named paronymously after what comes about through them.

raw_text: {"translation": "[382] First, then, and above all, one must make the test of the power being judged from the very thing with reference to which it is said. For if hemlock is cooling to a human being, it does not follow that it is so to a starling as well; nor, if it is nourishing to the starling, does it follow that it is so to a human being as well. In the same way, if hellebore is purgative, it does not follow that it is purgative of quails as well; nor, if it is nourishing to them, does it follow that it is so to human beings as well. Next, one must distinguish what is so by accident from what is so primarily and in itself. So too with respect to smell it must display no quality, in the way that some of the utterly bad waters strike the sense with sourness, or pungency, or brine, or putrefaction, or some other indescribable foulness. Water, then, that is free of all these is not itself exactly unmixed with respect to its nature, just as no other of the four perceptible elements is either; it is, however, unmixed as far as perception and use are concerned.

response.translation: This, then, is a most difficult matter, and one requiring much precision and practice. For in all such matters it is necessary to begin from experience, as has already been said, and to reason securely, taking care not to [430] entangle oneself in insoluble questions. For which reason one might well be astonished at those who have investigated such things, seeing them come to grief at their own hands in most of what they investigate and write, as Herodotus does. For, beginning from the whole of the most ancient record of compound drugs, they proceed to the examination of the simples contained in them. Since, say, vinegar has been mixed into these or those warming drugs, they thereupon declare it too to be hot. But it is not clear whether it has been rightly mixed in, before one has discovered its power on its own. raw_text: {"translation": "This very point could be settled in the following way, if one were to give [437] someone both wine and vinegar, each separately by itself. For the person is evidently always made thirstier by wine, whereas after drinking vinegar he is sometimes thirstier and sometimes less thirsty. This is because thirst itself also arises in two ways, the one from a deficiency of moisture, the other from an excess of heat. So it is no wonder if vinegar does not cure the former but does cure the other, for it cannot moisten, but it cools not ignobly. response.translation: To all the things that have been said about these there is an opposite affection, arising from an opposite cause, whenever the composition of what enters, in liquids, being by nature akin to the condition of the tongue, smooths by anointing the parts that have been roughened, and of the parts that are contrary to nature either compacted or diffused, the ones it [448] draws together, the others it relaxes, and settles all of them as far as possible according to nature: every such thing, becoming a remedy of the violent affections and being pleasant and agreeable to everyone, has been called sweet. Through this whole passage Plato explained which things it is customary to name harsh and which acerbic, which salty and nitrous and which bitter, and which pungent, which sour and which sweet; evidently calling 'harsh' what we call astringent, for so it was named among the ancient Greeks. He does not, however, confound everything into the same thing, as these people do, who say that pepper is astringent, although it belongs to the nature of the pungent, and vinegar, although it belongs to that of the sour, and who are not ashamed to assign even some of the sweetest things to the astringents. Since, then, everything is confounded by them, right at the outset not even powers can be discovered. For the starting-points of all discovery and demonstration are the things that are evident to perception and to understanding.

response.translation: Now by Theophrastus, Aristotle and Mnesitheus the physician, and those of their school, the gustatory power is named chymos, with the letter m beginning the [450] second syllable; but the consistency arising from moist and dry, when these have been concocted by heat, is named chylos, with l beginning the second syllable. Among their older predecessors, however, not only the Attic writers but also the Ionians, both are written with m. For it is found so in Plato the philosopher, in Hippocrates, and in the old comic poets. In the present treatise at any rate, for the sake of clear instruction, let us say that the gustatory power, or quality, or however one may wish to name it, is chymos, with the letter m, while the thickened moisture in animals and plants is chylos, with l beginning the second syllable. It must be understood, then, that the chymoi found in each plant and animal, and indeed also those found in the earth, are very numerous and not easily counted in their kinds (ἰδέαις). The gustatory differences among them, however, have seemed to some to be eight in number, to others seven, and to others even fewer than these.

response.translation: For it surely makes no difference whether one says 'sweet' or [452] 'honey-like', just as it makes none whether one says 'oily' or 'olive-oil-like'. But he has left out the oily as having nothing to do with taste. To express it precisely is not possible, since neither can any other of the perceptible affections be so expressed; but it is possible to remind someone who has shared in the same sensation. If anyone has ever tasted quinces, or apples, or myrtle-berries, or medlars, he knows clearly that the sensation arising in us on the tongue from these is one thing, and that from astringent bodies another. For astringent or cooling things appear to press the part of us that touches them inward evenly from every side, as if pushing, compressing and drawing it together; whereas harsh things seem both to penetrate into the depth and to bring on a rough and uneven sensation, as if drying up and grazing away all the moisture of the sensing bodies. So the particular character of the affections produced in us by astringent bodies and by harsh flavours is different, and it cannot even be stated clearly.

response.translation: But any man who has sense knows [453] what I mean. When the body that comes into contact with the tongue dries it vehemently, draws it together and roughens it to a greater depth, as unripe wild pears and cornels do, everything of this kind is called acerbic, differing from the harsh by intensity. What we call astringent, however, is scarcely to be found mentioned by Theophrastus and his school. It seems either to signify the same thing as the harsh, or to be a genus common to this and to the acerbic. Those things which, in touching the tongue, do not draw it together, nor constrict it as astringents do, but appear to do entirely the opposite, cleansing and washing away even whatever of the astringents may be lying upon it, all these we call salty. Those that cleanse still more than these, to the point of roughening it painfully, are called bitter. Those that are biting and corroding with strong heat are called pungent. Those that are biting without it are called sour, and to these belongs also the property of leavening.

response.translation: For it is clear that, if all things have been mixed from hot, cold, dry and moist coming together, each of the qualities mentioned also arises from the mixture [455] of these. If, then, they were to attempt to explain how each of the flavours mentioned comes about, I would gladly listen to them and would feel no small gratitude towards them. But if they do not even do this, and moreover confound all the perceptible differences into one and the same thing, so that they run the risk of calling all bodies astringent, I would not wish to listen to them, and I would pray that they too might cease from their vain contentiousness. But we, in what follows, shall try to show of what mixture each of the flavours is the offspring. For the present I wish only to accustom the learners, as they come to the test of experience, first to pick out just that which is useful for the art, whenever they wish to judge how each of the drugs disposes us. For we are certainly not examining what sort of thing it is in itself and in relation to nature as a whole. For it is clear that in this way neither vinegar nor sea-water could be said to dry us, or to be dry in power.

response.translation: [459] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK II. The sophists who overstep their proper bounds make our account of the power of simple drugs a long one. For by beginning from far back and slighting sense-perception, and by throwing themselves into questions that remain unresolved even among the philosophers, they ruin, along with the things they do not know, the things that are clearly known as well.
uncertain_greek: ΛΥΝΑΜΕΩς (a misprint for ΔΥΝΑΜΕΩΣ, taken as 'power')
προσαπολλύουσιν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσιν: the dative οἷς is taken as 'along with what they do not know'; it could also be instrumental, 'by means of what they do not know'
ἠπορημένα: taken as 'questions that remain unresolved', i.e. matters of aporia
